subject: Meaning of sampling statement in Stan

messages.author: 5849fb7df434dd76
messages.subject: Meaning of sampling statement in Stan
parts:
I have what I suspect is a very basic question about what a sampling statement really means in Stan.

For example, consider the following simple model (which is very similar to the first example in the "Regression Models - Linear Regression" section of the Stan reference:

// Save in OneFactorCrossSectional.stan
data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  vector[N] r;
  vector[N] sigma;
  real sigma_g;
}
parameters {
  real g;
}
model {
  r ~ normal(g, sigma); // (1)
  g ~ normal(0, sigma_g);
}

which we can run from R as follows:

library(rstan)

data <- data.frame(
  r     = c(0.2, 0.4),
  sigma = c(1,   2),
  g     = 1)

# Linear model ####
print(summary(lm(r ~ g + 0, data = data, weights = 1/data$sigma ^ 2)))

# STAN model ####
sigma_g <- 10
one.fac.fit <- stan('OneFactorCrossSectional.stan',
                    data = list(N = nrow(data),
                                r = data$r,
                                sigma = data$sigma,
                                sigma_g = sigma_g))

My question is about equation (1) in the Stan file: r ~ normal(g, sigma). My issue is that the LHS, "r", is a constant, so it seems odd to sample from it! I believe an equivalent version of this sampling statement is to replace (1) with (2), below:

0 ~ normal(g - r, sigma); // (2)

This appears to produce the same results as (1), but now we are expressing the distribution of 0, which seems even stranger (to me). The most natural way to write this (but bear in mind that I'm new to Stan) is as

g - r ~ normal(0, sigma); // (3)

Which also seems to produce the same results. Are these all equivalent? Why can we state what the distribution of a constant is?

One of my problems arising from these doubts, is what happens when things are a little more complicated. For example, suppose our model is that r is equal to g^2 (g squared) plus an error. Then the above examples suggest two ways to model it.  First we can follow the Stan reference, accept the peculiarity of stating what the distribution of a constant is, and write something like:

0 ~ normal(g*g - r, sigma); // (4)

This parses and compiles without warning, although sampling from the model generates many divergent transitions. An alternative approach, which seems more natural to me, is to write

g*g - r ~ normal(0, sigma); // (5)

This, of couse, generates a warning reminding us to add a term to the log prob. Is (4) equivalent to (5) plus a suitable increment to the log prob?

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Meaning of sampling statement in Stan
parts:
Every line with "~" in the model block in a Stan program is adding a term to the log-posterior density.  No sampling is done.
A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Meaning of sampling statement in Stan
parts:
Basic questions like this are all covered in gory detail in
the manual. In short,

y ~ foo(theta);

gets translated as roughly

target += foo_lpdf(y | theta);

where foo_lpdf is the density (or mass function it'll be _lpmf).

The answers to all of your questions derive from the
definition of foo_lpdf and what the variables are. See below.

- Bob

Yes, in terms of their effect on the target log density.

>> One of my problems arising from these doubts, is what happens when things are a little more complicated. For example, suppose our model is that r is equal to g^2 (g squared) plus an error. Then the above examples suggest two ways to model it. First we can follow the Stan reference, accept the peculiarity of stating what the distribution of a constant is, and write something like:
>>

>>

>>
>> g*g - r ~ normal(0, sigma); // (5)
>>
>> This, of couse, generates a warning reminding us to add a term to the log prob. Is (4) equivalent to (5) plus a suitable increment to the log prob?

These produce the same reuslt in terms of what gets added to
the target density, but conceptually these are very different.

If you're trying to use the second one to put a distribution on
transformed parmaeters, then you need the Jacobian adjustment.
If they're used as priors, you don't.

- Bob
